e.t: Abineem, also rendered Avineem, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears four times, all in Judges, where the English rendering is consistently “Abineem.” The name occurs in Judges 4:6 and 4:12, and again in Judges 5:1 and 5:12. Without the surrounding verse text, its main meaning is simply the personal name Abineem; the specific role or significance connected with the person must be understood from each passage.

This word is a proper name, rendered as “Angaiou; Anggeu.” It identifies a named person or place in the Greek Old Testament rather than expressing a general idea, action, or quality. It occurs nine times in nine verses within the Greek Old Testament, appearing in Ezra, Psalms, and Haggai. The available information establishes its naming function, but the surrounding verse text is needed to determine exactly whom or what the name identifies in each passage.

This word means “unborn.” It describes someone or something that has not been born, and it can function as an adjective or a noun. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, in Exodus, Deuteronomy, and Job. Its basic sense remains focused on the condition of not yet having been born; the surrounding verse determines how that condition is being discussed.

Azau is a proper name, also rendered “Azav,” identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament (LXX). Its meaning is therefore a personal designation rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It occurs once in this LXX corpus, at Genesis 22:22. The name and location are clear, but this information does not establish additional contextual significance beyond that single occurrence.

This verb means “salt”: to apply salt or make something salted. In the Greek Old Testament, it describes the action of adding salt rather than salt as an object or substance. It occurs twice in the Septuagint, in Leviticus 2:13 and Ezekiel 16:4. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but the central idea remains the use or application of salt.

This noun means “sea-water” or “brine,” referring to salty water rather than fresh water. It names the substance itself and carries a concrete, ordinary meaning. In the LXX corpus, it occurs two times, appearing once in Psalms and once in Sirach. The word therefore describes a kind of water by its saltiness and connection with the sea, while the precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This noun means a vineyard: land planted and cultivated for grapevines. It names a real agricultural place rather than the vines or grapes themselves. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 89 times, showing that vineyards are a familiar part of biblical descriptions of land, work, ownership, harvest, and daily life. Its earliest recorded occurrence is in Genesis 9:20, and it continues through Song of Songs 8:12. The word is rendered “vineyard” in the available translation evidence.

This adjective describes something that provides no benefit, produces no useful result, or is of no practical value. It can be expressed as “unprofitable” or “useless,” pointing to the lack of worthwhile outcome rather than merely describing something difficult or unpleasant. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times, in Wisdom and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on what the surrounding passage identifies as having no benefit or use.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “wipe out”: to remove something so that it is gone. It describes decisive clearing away rather than merely moving or covering something. The word occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, including passages from Genesis, 2 Kings, Isaiah, Daniel, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being removed, but its central idea remains complete eradication or removal.

This Greek LXX verb means “emancipate”: to release someone from a condition of bondage or dependence and allow that person to live as free. It describes an action done to another person rather than a general state of freedom. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Leviticus 19:20. The precise force of the word in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its legal context, but its central meaning remains the act of setting someone free.

This verb means “part,” referring to separating or dividing something. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice—once in Daniel and once in 2 Maccabees—so its ordinary meaning is clear, while the exact force in each passage depends on the surrounding sentence. The word does not by itself specify whether the division concerns people, possessions, territory, or another object; the context identifies what is being parted.

This Greek LXX verb describes beating someone to death with a cudgel or club, and it can also refer to bastinado—beating the soles of the feet. It therefore expresses a violent act of killing or severe physical punishment, rather than an ordinary beating. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, once in Daniel and once in 3 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative context.

This is the proper name Arioch, identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament text of Daniel. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but a personal designation. The name appears twice in the Greek Daniel, in Daniel 2:14 and Daniel 2:15. Its precise role in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the person’s name, Arioch.

This word means “this moment” or “just now”. It is an adverb that points to the present time, marking something happening at the current moment rather than at an earlier or later time. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it appears eleven times, including passages in Daniel and 2 Maccabees. Its basic force remains focused and immediate: it directs attention to what is true, happening, or being said at that point in time. The surrounding words determine exactly what present circumstance it highlights.

Aphalēl, also rendered Afalil, is a proper name referring to a person. It is not a common word that describes an action, quality, or object, so its meaning is primarily its identity as a personal name. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 1 Chronicles 2:37. The available record does not provide surrounding verse text, so the name itself can be explained clearly, while the person’s specific role must be determined from the passage.

This adjective describes someone or something free from envy—that is, not resentful of another person’s good, honor, or prosperity. It presents an attitude marked by generous, unjealous goodwill rather than rivalry or ill feeling. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus represented here, once in 3 Maccabees and once in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains straightforward: without envy.

Balak, also rendered Valak, is a proper name for a person in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies the king associated especially with the events recorded in Numbers, where the name appears most often. The word itself functions as a personal designation rather than a general description, action, or quality. It occurs 53 times in the Greek Old Testament, from Genesis through Micah. Its precise significance in any individual verse comes from the surrounding passage and the person being named.

This word means “monarch” or “king”—a male ruler who holds authority over a people or kingdom. It is a noun used for an individual ruler and can also refer to kings in the plural or to something belonging to a king. In the Greek Old Testament, it is broadly used, appearing 3,008 times from Genesis through Song of Songs. Its ordinary sense remains focused on royal rule and the person who exercises it.

This Greek verb means “help”: it describes giving assistance to someone who needs support. As a verb, it expresses an action—coming to another’s aid—rather than a person, place, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs 101 times, making it a well-established word for acts of assistance across many passages. Its exact force in any verse depends on who is helping and what need is being addressed.

Ganoza is a proper name, functioning as a personal or identifying name rather than a word that describes an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Chronicles 36:8. The available lexical information preserves the name itself but does not provide a further definition or explain whether it identifies a person, place, or another named subject. Its precise reference therefore depends on the verse context.

Gesir, also rendered Yesir, is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It does not describe an action, quality, or general idea; it functions as an individual name. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 2 Samuel 3:3. The available wording establishes the name itself, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain the person’s role or significance in that passage.

“Gēzam” or “Yizam” is a proper name preserved in the Greek Old Testament text. It appears once in the Greek Septuagint, in Nehemiah 7:51. The available information identifies this entry as a name rather than a general concept, action, quality, or object. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific referent cannot be described further. Its ordinary meaning is therefore the personal or family designation represented by “Gēzam” or “Yizam.”

Debbōra is a proper name, rendered also as Thevvora. It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs eleven times in eleven verses: once in Genesis and ten times in Judges. Its repeated use in Judges identifies the woman known as Debbōra, while its occurrence in Genesis identifies another person bearing the same name. The name itself does not provide a general definition beyond functioning as a personal name.

This word means “bundle,” referring to several things gathered or tied together as one group. It is a noun, so it names the gathered object rather than an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Exodus 12:22. The basic meaning is clear, while the surrounding verse gives the specific object being gathered. Its use fits ordinary language for something collected into a single tied group.

This verb means “malign”: to speak against someone in a harmful or damaging way. It describes an active act of attacking another person’s reputation or character through hostile speech. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, it occurs three times—once in Daniel and twice in Maccabees. Because the available information does not include the surrounding verse text, the precise force of each occurrence must be understood from its sentence and passage. Its central sense remains the act of maligning or speaking against someone.

This Greek LXX noun means “disposition” or “arrangement”: the way something is set in order, organized, or placed. It can describe an established arrangement rather than an action itself. The word occurs nine times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, including Esther, Psalms, and the Maccabean books. Its exact shade of meaning depends on what is being arranged or ordered in the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains a disposition or orderly arrangement.

This verb means “spread,” describing the action of laying something out across a surface or area. It presents spreading as an action rather than naming an object or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Samuel 9:25. The word’s basic sense is clear from its definition, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain exactly what was spread and why in that passage.

This Greek LXX verb expresses the idea of transcending something—going beyond it—or transporting something from one place to another. Its meaning therefore depends on what it governs: it can describe superiority or surpassing, and it can also describe carrying or conveying. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented here, it occurs 13 times, so it is used across more than one setting rather than having only a single specialized sense. Its lexical definition is “transcend; transport.”

This Greek LXX noun means “justification.” It refers to justification as a recognized matter of being declared or treated rightly. The word appears 136 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so it is used broadly rather than being limited to one passage or setting. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea remains justification. The word occurs especially often in Psalms and Deuteronomy, where language about what is right, required, or accepted is prominent.

This word means “gift”: something given or presented to another person, whether as an offering, possession, or benefit. It is a noun, so it names the thing being given rather than the act of giving. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, it occurs 50 times, including passages concerning gifts brought to God, possessions given to others, and gifts received. Its central idea remains a tangible or granted gift, while the surrounding passage determines who gives it and why.

This noun means “defamation”: speech or claims that damage another person’s reputation. It refers to dishonoring someone through damaging words, rather than simply expressing disagreement or criticism. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, in 1 Maccabees 7:38 and 3 Maccabees 2:26. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain how the word operates in either passage, but its basic sense remains the act or charge of speaking against someone in a reputation-damaging way.

This Greek LXX verb means “allow” or “let”: it expresses giving permission for someone or something to happen, or calling for that permission to be given. It can therefore function as a direct request, command, or statement about permitting an action, depending on the sentence. The word occurs 22 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, from Genesis through 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding words.

It means “as a whole nation,” describing people considered together as one national body rather than as separate individuals or smaller groups. As an adverb, it modifies an action or statement by showing that the action applies collectively to the nation. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it appears once, in 4 Maccabees 2:19. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse text, which is not included here.

This verb means to “scrape out” or “obliterate,” describing the removal or complete wiping away of something. It is a Greek LXX word and appears once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, at Exodus 36:13. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The central idea is forceful removal: something is scraped out until it is gone, or obliterated so that it no longer remains. The precise force in that verse depends on its surrounding wording.

Elasa is a proper name rendered as “Elasa.” It functions as a name identifying a person, place, or other named entity, though the available information does not specify which in each passage. This name occurs three times in the Greek LXX corpus: in 1 Chronicles 8:37, Jeremiah 48:1, and 1 Maccabees 9:5. Its precise referent depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic lexical meaning is the name Elasa itself.

Eliaba, also rendered Eliava, is a personal name. It functions as a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 11:33. The available lexical information identifies the name but does not provide a separate descriptive meaning or etymological explanation. Its precise significance in that verse must therefore be understood from the surrounding passage, not from the name alone.

This verb means “stain”: to mark or soil something so that it is no longer clean. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 24:9. That single occurrence identifies the word’s limited use in this corpus, while its basic meaning remains the act of staining or defiling. The precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

This noun means “breathing,” referring to the act or process of drawing breath. It names a physical function rather than an action someone performs in a particular sentence. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalms 17:16. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain its precise force there, but its basic meaning remains the intake or movement of breath.

This verb means “string on,” describing the act of putting something onto a string or similar support. It is a simple action word rather than a title, quality, or abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears only once, at Job 10:11. The reference identifies its location, while the surrounding verse text is needed to explain exactly what is being strung on there.

This noun means “investigation”—the careful examination or searching out of something. It describes a process of looking closely in order to discover, understand, or establish what is true. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Psalm 63:7. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s precise emphasis in that passage must be determined from its context; its basic meaning remains a deliberate inquiry or careful investigation.

This Greek LXX preposition means “in” or “on.” It connects a person, thing, or action with the place, surface, or setting where it is situated. The precise English wording depends on what follows it, but its central idea is position or relation to something. It is very common in the Greek LXX, occurring 6,662 times, so it serves a wide range of ordinary sentence connections rather than naming a person, object, or action by itself.

This Greek LXX verb means “added strength to; confirmed.” It describes strengthening someone or something, and it can also express making something firm or established. As a verb, it points to an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Ecclesiastes 4:12. The exact force in that verse depends on its surrounding wording, but its central idea remains reinforcement: what is weak is made stronger, or what is uncertain is confirmed.

This verb means to furnish oneself with food—to obtain or provide what one needs to eat. It describes a person’s action rather than food itself, and its wording points to personal provision. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 9:4. The surrounding verse text is not available here, so the word’s basic meaning can be stated confidently, while its precise force in that sentence belongs to the wider passage.

Eseraēl, also rendered Eserel, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 4:16, identifying a person. Because the available record supplies the name but not the surrounding verse text, its significance in that genealogy must be understood from the passage itself. The name’s normal function is simply to identify the individual called Eserel.

This verb means to be last or to come too late. It describes arriving after the proper or expected time, or being at the end of a sequence. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 5:53. The surrounding verse text is not available here, so the word’s specific force in that sentence must be determined from its context. Its basic idea remains lateness or being last.

This adjective describes something that melts readily or is easily dissolved by heat. It points to a material lacking resistance to melting, rather than describing an action performed by a person. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Wisdom 19:21. Its precise application there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the word itself carries the straightforward idea of being easily melted.

Esam, also rendered Isam, is a proper name for a person rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, appearing in Ezra and Nehemiah. The name identifies individuals in those genealogical or community records, but the available information does not establish a broader meaning beyond the personal name itself. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person being named.

“Thanaach; Thanaakh” is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament wording preserved by the Septuagint. It identifies a named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship, so its meaning is primarily the name itself, not a general concept. It occurs once in this Greek Old Testament corpus, in Judges 5:19. Without the verse text, the name alone does not establish additional details about the person, place, or event it identifies.

This noun means “sulfur,” the distinctive mineral substance named in the Greek Old Testament and related Jewish writings. It refers to a tangible material rather than an action, person, or quality. The word occurs 15 times in the Greek LXX corpus, across Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This Greek LXX noun means “warmth” or “heat”—the condition of being warm or intensely hot. It names physical heat rather than an action, person, or abstract quality. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in Jeremiah and once in Daniel. One English rendering is “heat,” which confirms this basic sense. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

Idedi, also called Ithethi, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It functions as the name of an individual in the Greek Old Testament. This name occurs once in the LXX, at 2 Samuel 12:25. Because no verse text or surrounding passage is provided here, the name itself does not support further conclusions about the person or the event in which he appears.

Ierioth is a proper name, identifying a named individual or figure rather than expressing an action, quality, or object. Its recorded meaning is “Ieriōth; Ierioth,” which functions as a name rather than a translatable description. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 2:18. The name’s specific significance in that passage depends on the verse and surrounding genealogy, which are not included here.

This verb means “be rusty.” It describes something as becoming rusty or being in a rusty condition. As a verb, it expresses an action or state rather than naming an object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in Sirach. Its ordinary sense concerns rust and the condition produced by corrosion; the precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording. The word’s lexical meaning is therefore straightforward: to be rusty.

Israel is the name “Israel,” and it can also describe something as “of Israel.” In the Greek Old Testament, this noun is used very frequently, with 2,592 occurrences beginning in Genesis and continuing through Song of Songs. Its normal function is to identify Israel or mark something in relation to Israel, rather than express an action or quality. The precise reference in any verse depends on its surrounding context.

This verb means “sit” or “set”: it describes taking a seated position or placing something in position, according to how it functions in a sentence. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Exodus 12:22. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the exact force of the word in that occurrence cannot be stated more specifically. Its central idea remains sitting or setting something in place.

This verb means “boast against” or “exult over,” describing the act of proudly lifting oneself above someone else or celebrating superiority over them. It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than naming a person or thing. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all within three verses. Its central idea remains the proud expression of triumph or superiority directed against another. The surrounding passage determines who is boasting and whom the boasting is directed against.

This Greek LXX verb means “throw down.” It describes the act of causing someone or something to fall from a higher place or position. As a verb, it expresses forceful downward movement rather than simply being below or moving downward voluntarily. The word occurs four times in the Greek LXX corpus, including three occurrences in deuterocanonical books and one in 2 Chronicles. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and situation.

This Greek LXX noun means a “voyage” or “trip,” referring to travel from one place to another. It describes the journey itself rather than a person, destination, or particular means of travel. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 3 Maccabees 4:10. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain its precise role in that passage, but its basic meaning is a journey or voyage.

This adjective describes something held in possession—that is, kept as someone’s property or belonging. It presents the thing as possessed or owned rather than merely noticed, used, or temporarily received. In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears once, in Leviticus 25:46. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains something under a person’s possession or control.

This word means ivy, the climbing plant that grows along surfaces and can spread over walls or trees. It is a noun naming the plant itself. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 6:7. The word’s basic meaning is straightforward: it identifies ivy rather than an abstract quality, action, or person. Its precise significance in that occurrence depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are needed to explain how the plant is being mentioned there.

This word means an itch—an irritating sensation felt on the skin that creates a desire to scratch. It is a noun, naming the physical discomfort itself rather than an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Deuteronomy 28:27, so its basic meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not available here. Its precise force in that passage depends on the context in which the bodily condition is mentioned.

This Greek LXX verb means “exhausted” or “abate”: it describes something becoming spent, weakening, or calming down. It can refer to strength running out, or to a force such as wind or turmoil losing intensity. The word appears 26 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its precise nuance depends on what is becoming less active or powerful in each passage. Its first recorded occurrence is in Genesis 8:1.

This adjective means “like a beast” or “brutish,” describing someone or something marked by animal-like lack of understanding or refinement. It presents a person as behaving without the thoughtful discernment normally associated with human wisdom. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Psalm 72:22. Its exact force in that verse is clarified by the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is a comparison to beast-like behavior or condition.

This noun means “hurricane,” referring to a powerful, violent storm. It names a force of nature rather than an action, person, or spiritual quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs seven times, including passages in Job, Jeremiah, Wisdom, and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains a destructive, turbulent storm. The word appears in both Old Testament and deuterocanonical Greek material.

This word means “remnant”: what is left after a larger part has been removed, lost, or gone. As a noun, it identifies a remaining portion or group rather than the whole. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in 2 Samuel 21:2 and 2 Kings 19:4, and its meaning is rendered consistently as “remnant.” The surrounding passage determines exactly what remains in each occurrence, but the word itself points plainly to what is left over from something larger.

This LXX word means “pestilence” or “pest,” referring to a harmful affliction or a person regarded as troublesome. It can function as a noun, naming the danger or nuisance itself, and its adjective use can describe someone or something associated with such trouble. The word occurs 27 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, so it is used across a range of passages rather than being limited to one setting. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

Mala is a proper name, rendered as “Mala.” It functions as a identifying name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, it occurs 11 times, across both Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Because no verse text or surrounding context is available here, its specific referent must be determined from the individual passage where the name appears.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Manochō; Manokho,” rather than a common term describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named figure or place in the Greek Old Testament tradition, though the available information does not specify which. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Joshua 15:59. Its precise referent must therefore be identified from that passage’s surrounding text.

This Greek LXX noun means a mixture or compound: something formed by combining different ingredients or parts. It can describe a blended preparation rather than a single, unmixed substance. The word occurs once in the Greek text of the deuterocanonical books, at Sirach 38:7. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea is a combined substance or preparation. The word therefore points to what has been brought together into one mixture or compound.

This verb expresses concern or care for someone or something—what matters enough to receive attention. It can describe an active interest rather than mere awareness, so the sense is that a person takes something seriously or looks after it. The word appears 20 times in the Greek LXX corpus represented here, across both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains concern or care. [p03:word:lxx:L708696:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L708696:occurrences]

This Greek LXX verb means being “alone.” It describes a person who is by himself or without others, expressing solitary existence rather than companionship. As a verb, it presents being alone as a condition or state. This word occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Psalm 101:8. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but its basic meaning remains clear: to be alone.

This word means “mill,” referring to a device used to grind grain or other material. It is a noun, so it names the object rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 52:11. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain exactly how the mill is being mentioned there, but the word itself carries the ordinary meaning of a mill. Its basic sense is therefore concrete and practical: a grinding device used in daily life.

This word is a proper name, appearing in the Greek Old Testament as “Nabouchodonosor” or “Navukhothonosor.” It identifies the same named person across passages in Kings, Chronicles, Ezra, Esther, Jeremiah, Daniel, and the Epistle of Jeremiah. The name occurs 68 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical writings, so its meaning is primarily the personal name itself rather than a general description or action.

Nacheth or Nakheth is a proper name used for a person in the Greek Old Testament. It does not describe an action, quality, or spiritual concept; it identifies someone by name. This LXX word occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 1:37, within a genealogical listing. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, its personal identity is the clear lexical meaning.

This word expresses that something is to be regarded or reckoned in a certain way—“one must account; deem.” It functions as an adjective, describing what ought to be considered or counted. In its Greek LXX usage, it appears four times, all in the Epistle of Jeremiah. The word therefore carries a sense of required judgment or estimation: something must be treated as deserving a particular account or evaluation. Its precise force in each occurrence depends on the surrounding verse and sentence.

Ommoth is a proper name preserved in the Greek Septuagint (LXX). It functions as a personal or place name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. The available lexical meaning is simply “Ommōth,” also rendered “Ommoth.” It occurs once in the Greek LXX, at Numbers 25:15. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself does not establish whether Ommoth refers to a person or a location; that identification belongs to the passage context.

e.h: A Proper Name: Orē or Ori
e.t: This word is a proper name: “Orē” or “Ori.” It identifies a named referent rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. Because it appears in the Greek Septuagint as a proper noun, its precise referent must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage. It occurs 100 times in the LXX corpus, including Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so the name appears across many passages without changing its basic naming function.

“Fortifying” means the process of making a place or defense stronger, especially by building or strengthening its protective works. As a noun, this word names the work itself rather than the person who carries it out. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both in 1 Maccabees. It may refer to fortification as an ongoing activity or completed work, while the surrounding verse determines the particular setting.

gl: all-variegated; of rich and varied work
d: all-variegated; of rich and varied work

e.t: This adjective describes something “all-variegated” or “of rich and varied work”—something marked by many colors, patterns, or forms of skilled workmanship. It is a descriptive word, so it portrays the character or appearance of a person, object, or work rather than naming an action. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 4 Maccabees 15:11; the surrounding verse is needed to know exactly what it describes there.

This Greek LXX noun means “advent” or “arrival,” referring to someone coming or being present. It describes the event of a person’s arrival rather than an action performed by the person. In this deuterocanonical Greek corpus, it occurs three times: twice in 2 Maccabees and once in 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence and context.

This noun means “sole,” referring to the underside of the foot. It names a physical part of the body rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Esther 4:17. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context, but its ordinary meaning is the sole or bottom surface of the foot.
